---
title: "From question to cohort"
description: >
  Turn a research question into a table of entries, one row per person, by
  selecting records on the database and choosing entries in R.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

A research question is about people: who they are, what happened to them and
when. THIP holds records. This guide turns one question into rows: it stacks the
yearly tables, checks their dates, selects the matching records on the database
and, in R, chooses one entry for each person.

The question, which the next guides carry on, is:

> Among people admitted with appendicitis, how many are readmitted within 30
> days of discharge, and is that more common in people with diabetes?

Here you build its starting point: the people admitted with appendicitis, one
row each, with the dates that the next guide measures from.

The map below is the whole guide in one picture. Rules that judge each record
on its own, such as "is this an appendicitis admission in the study period?",
run on the database, so only the matching records travel to R. Choosing each
person's entry compares their records with each other; there are few of them by
then, so that runs in R, where you can look at every row. What comes into R is
small: counts, the date-audit summary, a few rows to look at, and the candidate
records.

```{r cohort-pipeline, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Inline, so the diagram travels with the page and keeps its title and description.
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/cohort-pipeline.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

As in [Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html), every example runs on the
example database of invented records; on THIP, connect with `thip_connect()`
instead.

```{r connect}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()
```

## Words for a cohort

A few words name the pieces of a cohort. This course uses each in one sense:

- **Person:** one `pid`. Your question is about people; the tables hold records.
- **Source population:** the people your tables can see. THIP's inpatient
  tables hold hospital stays with claims paid through NHSO ([Meet the THIP
  data](meet-the-data.html)), so your results describe those people. Here,
  anyone with such a record in fiscal years 2565 to 2567.
- **Study period:** the dates on which an admission can bring someone into the
  study. Here, admissions from 1 October 2021 to 31 August 2024.
- **Candidate record:** a record that passes the selection rules: admitted in
  the study period, with a principal diagnosis of appendicitis. One person can
  have several.
- **Entry:** the one candidate record chosen to bring a person into the study,
  here their first. Its `tran_id` becomes the entry's `entry_id`.
- **Index date:** the date you measure time from. This question needs two: the
  look-back for history such as diabetes runs up to admission (`adm_date`), and
  the 30 days of follow-up start at discharge (`dsc_date`).

The cohort is the table of entries, one row per person. This guide calls it
`entries`.

## Stack the tables, convert the dates

In the example, the study period's admissions sit in three yearly tables, so
you stack three. As in [Working with a database from R](database-from-r.html),
`thip_table()` stacks tables of the same kind, with the same columns, into one
query with SQL's `UNION ALL`. It keeps every row as it is, without removing
duplicates or merging records, and `.id` adds a column naming the table each
row came from.

Dates are text, so `thip_table()` can also convert them as it stacks.
`dates = c(adm = "dateadm")` makes a new column `adm` from the text column
`dateadm`; `date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d")` says how to read it. In a format,
`%Y` is the four-digit year, `%m` the month and `%d` the day. Nothing is
guessed: `dateadm` and `datedsc` look like `20231015`, which is `"%Y%m%d"`, and
`death_date` looks like `2023-10-15`, which is `"%Y-%m-%d"`.

This is the `admissions` query the course builds on; the next guides leave out
`death`:

```{r admissions}
admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc", death = "death_date"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d", death = "%Y-%m-%d")
)
```

Look at three records that have a death date, so that both formats show:

```{r admissions-print}
admissions |>
  filter(death_date != "") |>
  select(source_table, dateadm, adm, datedsc, dsc, death_date, death) |>
  head(3)
```

Both raw styles, `20220605` and `2022-06-12`, become the same `<date>` values.
Each converted column sits beside its raw text, which stays for checking.
`admissions` is still a query: the conversion runs on the database whenever you
use it, and printing fetched only these three rows. In the example, a death
date can fall after the last admission in the tables; on THIP, check the range
of `death_date` before you use it.

A value that cannot be read as a date becomes `NA`: a blank, text in another
format, a day that does not exist such as 30 February, or a year outside 1900
to 2299. If the text holds a time as well, give a format with the time, such as
`"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"`: the new date column then keeps the calendar day and drops
the time. With `"%Y-%m-%d"` alone, such text becomes `NA`. thipR also reads
`"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%OS"`, with seconds of up to three decimals.

You can give a single format for every column, as `date_format = "%Y%m%d"`, but
only when they all share it: here it would turn every death date into `NA`, and
the audit below would count them as `n_failed`. For timestamp columns,
`thip_table()` also has `datetimes` and `datetime_format`. They need a
`timezone` you have confirmed with the data provider (thipR never guesses one),
and they run on THIP, not on the example database; see [its reference
page](../reference/thip_table.html).

Before you rely on the stack, check which admissions each table holds:

```{r table-span}
admissions |>
  group_by(source_table) |>
  summarise(records = n(), first_adm = min(adm, na.rm = TRUE),
            last_adm = max(adm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(source_table)
```

In the example, each table holds the admissions of its fiscal year, and the
last admission is on 30 September 2024. The last admission date tells you where
the data end, which sets how late the study period can run (see below). On
THIP, run the same check on the tables just before and after your study period
too, and stack any table that also holds admissions from your study period.

## Audit the dates before you filter

A filter on `adm` or `dsc` quietly drops every record whose date failed to
convert, so look for failures first. `thip_date_audit()` compares each raw
column with its converted one and counts, for each column, the values that were
missing (no value at all: `NULL` on the database, `NA` in R), blank (empty
text, `""`), parsed (read as a date) or failed (text that could not be read as
a date); the four add up to `n_total`. `n_inconsistent` counts converted dates
whose raw text was missing or blank, so anything above zero needs checking.

The audit runs summarising queries on the database, so only the counts come
into R. It reads every value in each column, which takes time on large tables,
so audit only the tables you will use. Group by something broad, such as the
source table: grouping by `pid` would bring back one row per person, which is
slow and brings person-level data into R. Audit the three date columns, table
by table:

```{r date-audit}
date_audit <- thip_date_audit(
  admissions,
  columns = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc", death = "death_date"),
  by = "source_table"
)

date_audit |>
  arrange(match(field, c("adm", "dsc", "death")), source_table) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Every admission date was read. Discharge dates have two failures in `nhso2566`
and one blank in `nhso2565`. Most death dates are blank, which here means no
death date, not a fault. A date that was read is a real calendar date, not
necessarily a correct one.

## Look at the failures

The audit says how many; to see which, keep the records whose converted
discharge date is missing and look at the raw text:

```{r failures}
admissions |>
  filter(is.na(dsc)) |>
  select(source_table, pdx, dateadm, datedsc, dsc) |>
  arrange(source_table, dateadm) |>
  collect()
```

Two discharge dates read `20230229`, 29 February 2023, a day that did not
exist; the other is blank. thipR does not repair them; you decide what they mean
for your study. Here, follow-up starts at discharge, so a record without a
discharge date cannot be an entry. None of these three is an appendicitis
record (look at `pdx`), so in the example the rule will remove nothing. Keep it
anyway: on THIP it applies wherever a discharge date fails, and it belongs in
your methods.

## Count as you go

Each selection step drops records. Count records and people after every step:
the counts are the flow chart your report needs, and a step that drops more
than you expect deserves a look. This small function counts both, on the
database or in R, and labels the step. Start with the source population:

```{r count-step}
count_step <- function(data, step) {
  data |>
    summarise(records = n(), people = n_distinct(pid)) |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(step = step, .before = records)
}

funnel <- count_step(admissions, "Source population: all admissions")
funnel
```

The three tables hold 9,827 records from 3,000 people. `collect()` does nothing
to a data frame already in R, so the same function counts a query or a data
frame.

## Select the candidate records

Two rules pick the candidates, and both are checked record by record on the
database:

- **Study period:** admitted from 1 October 2021 to 31 August 2024. The
  example's last admission is on 30 September 2024; stopping a month earlier
  leaves room for 30 days of follow-up after discharge, which you check once
  the entries are built. The look-back needs room too: an entry admitted in
  October 2021 has no earlier table to look back into. [Look back and follow
  up](look-back-follow-up.html) shows how to check that and what to do about
  it.
- **Principal diagnosis:** `pdx` starting with K35, acute appendicitis in
  ICD-10. The code list is yours; thipR supplies no clinical definitions.

`thip_filter_icd()` adds the diagnosis rule to the query. You choose the columns
it searches, `cols`, and how codes match: `"exact"` matches whole codes, and
`"prefix"` matches every code that starts with one of yours, so `K35` finds
K352, K353, K358 and so on. Before comparing, it ignores case, dots and the
spaces around each code; blank codes never match. Ranges such as `K35-K37` give
an error rather than a guess, so list each code. It keeps the matching records
as they are: it adds no columns and counts no people.

Add both rules to `admissions`; nothing runs yet:

```{r select}
in_period <- admissions |>
  filter(adm >= as.Date("2021-10-01"), adm <= as.Date("2024-08-31"))

selected <- in_period |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "K35", cols = "pdx", match = "prefix")
```

Add the two selection steps to the funnel; these counts still run on the
database:

```{r funnel-select}
funnel <- bind_rows(
  funnel,
  count_step(in_period, "Admitted in the study period"),
  count_step(selected, "Principal diagnosis K35")
)
funnel
```

The study period removes 270 records, those admitted in September 2024; the
diagnosis rule leaves 250 records from 250 people.

## Which codes matched {.tabset}

The two tabs count the selected records by principal diagnosis, one in dplyr and
one in SQL; use whichever you know.

### dplyr

```{r select-count}
selected |>
  count(pdx) |>
  arrange(pdx)
```

### SQL

This SQL stacks the tables with `UNION ALL`, cleans each code before comparing
it, and compares the admission dates as text: `YYYYMMDD` text sorts in date order,
and the audit showed that every `dateadm` is a valid date.

```{r select-sql}
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT pdx, count(*) AS n
  FROM (SELECT dateadm, pdx FROM nhso2565
        UNION ALL SELECT dateadm, pdx FROM nhso2566
        UNION ALL SELECT dateadm, pdx FROM nhso2567)
  WHERE dateadm BETWEEN '20211001' AND '20240831'
    AND upper(replace(trim(pdx), '.', '')) LIKE 'K35%'
  GROUP BY pdx
  ORDER BY pdx")
```

## What the filter caught

The four counts add up to 250 records; notice `k358`, an appendicitis code
written in lower case. A plain comparison misses it:

```{r plain-filter}
in_period |>
  filter(substr(pdx, 1, 3) == "K35") |>
  summarise(records = n())
```

That is one record short, because the comparison is case-sensitive.
`thip_filter_icd()` cleans each code before comparing, so it found all 250.
To search secondary diagnoses as well, add their columns:
`cols = c("pdx", paste0("sdx", 1:20))`. This question is about the principal
diagnosis only.

## Other eligibility rules

A real protocol also has eligibility rules, such as age. `age_y` is age in whole
years; THIP's dictionary does not say on which date it is measured, so check
this before you use it as age at admission. To count the selected records of
people aged 15 or over:

```{r age-rule}
selected |>
  filter(as.integer(age_y) >= 15) |>
  summarise(records = n(), people = n_distinct(pid))
```

19 of the 250 records are of people under 15. This guide keeps all ages; if
your protocol needs the rule, add it to `selected`:
`selected <- selected |> filter(as.integer(age_y) >= 15)`.

Decide whether such a rule applies before or after you choose each person's
first admission, because the order can change who enters. Take someone admitted
with appendicitis at 14 and again at 16. Apply the age rule first and the
admission at 16 becomes their entry; choose the first admission first and the
rule then drops them.

## Collect the candidates

The selection is small, so bring it into R:

```{r candidates}
candidates <- collect(selected)
```

`candidates` is now an ordinary data frame with one row per candidate record.
Check whether anyone has more than one:

```{r candidates-per-person}
candidates |>
  count(pid, name = "records") |>
  count(records, name = "people")
```

In the example, every person has one candidate record. Check this on THIP too:
a person can be admitted with appendicitis more than once, and then the next
step has to choose.

## Choose one entry per person

Each person enters once, at their first appendicitis admission with a discharge
date. To choose it, drop candidates without a discharge date, sort each
person's candidates by admission date and keep the first:

```{r entries}
entries <- candidates |>
  filter(!is.na(dsc)) |>
  arrange(pid, adm, tran_id) |>
  distinct(pid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(pid, entry_id = tran_id, adm_date = adm, dsc_date = dsc)

entries |>
  head(3)
```

`distinct()` keeps each person's first row in the sorted order, and
`.keep_all = TRUE` keeps every column, not only `pid`; `select()` then keeps
four of them and renames three as it goes, such as `entry_id = tran_id`.
Sorting by `tran_id` after the admission date breaks ties between two
admissions on the same day in a fixed way, so the same entries come out every
time you run it on the same data. `entry_id` keeps the record's `tran_id`, so
you can go back to the record in the same tables.

Check that there is one row per person, and that 30 days after the last
discharge is still on or before the last admission date in the tables, because
a readmission is found by its admission date:

```{r entries-check}
last_adm <- admissions |>
  summarise(last = max(adm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(last)

entries |>
  summarise(entries = n(), people = n_distinct(pid),
            followup_end = max(dsc_date) + 30, last_adm = last_adm)
```

There are as many entries as people. The last follow-up ends on 7 September
2024, before the last admission in the data, on 30 September 2024.

## The funnel

Add the last two steps and look at the whole funnel:

```{r funnel}
funnel <- bind_rows(
  funnel,
  count_step(filter(candidates, !is.na(dsc)), "With a discharge date"),
  count_step(entries, "Entries: first per person")
)
funnel
```

The first three rows were counted on the database, the last two in R. Each row
shows how many records and people a rule left; the last row counts entries, one
per person. In the example, nothing is lost after the diagnosis rule. On THIP,
these rows are where you would see how many records each rule removed, and they
are the numbers for your flow chart.

## The whole recipe

Here is everything this guide built, in one chunk; the next guide starts from
it:

```{r recipe}
admissions <- thip_table(
  con, tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"), .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d")
)

candidates <- admissions |>
  filter(adm >= as.Date("2021-10-01"), adm <= as.Date("2024-08-31")) |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "K35", cols = "pdx", match = "prefix") |>
  collect()

entries <- candidates |>
  filter(!is.na(dsc)) |>
  arrange(pid, adm, tran_id) |>
  distinct(pid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(pid, entry_id = tran_id, adm_date = adm, dsc_date = dsc)
```

## In short

- Name the pieces first: person, source population, study period, candidate
  record, entry and index date.
- `thip_table()` stacks yearly tables with the same columns into one query,
  keeps every row, and with `.id` records each row's table.
- Convert dates with an explicit format for each column. The raw text stays,
  `admissions` is still a query that runs on the database, and dates that
  cannot be read become `NA`.
- Run `thip_date_audit()` before you filter on a converted date, and decide
  what a missing date means for your study.
- Select candidates on the database with `filter()` and `thip_filter_icd()`,
  which matches whole codes or prefixes after cleaning case, dots and the
  spaces around each code.
- Collect the candidates and choose one entry per person in R.
- Count records and people after every step.

Next: [Look back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html) fetches the records
around each entry: `followup`, the admissions in the 30 days after discharge,
and `history`, the year before admission.

```{r disconnect, include = FALSE}
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```
